# Turning the Puzzle Inside Out: Why Counting Jigsaw Solutions Survives Every Flip

*A jigsaw puzzle can be built to encode any logic problem. Swap every tab for a blank and every blank for a tab and you get a new puzzle. It is a different object, yet it has exactly the same number of solutions. This is the story of why that holds, what it hides, and where the counting breaks.*

---

## A puzzle that is secretly a logic problem

Picture a wooden frame with a row of $n$ empty slots called *sockets*. Each socket takes one of two small pieces. One carries a protruding **tab**, which we write as $1$. The other carries an indented **blank**, which we write as $0$. Choosing a piece for every socket gives a string of $n$ bits,
$$a = (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) \in \{0,1\}^n .$$

Next to the frame lies a pile of larger *clause pieces*. Each clause piece has a few connectors along its edge. A connector is cut to reach one particular socket $i$ and is milled for one particular polarity $p$, either tab or blank. The connector *mates* when the piece sitting in socket $i$ has exactly that polarity, that is, when $a_i = p$. A clause piece snaps into the frame as soon as **at least one** of its connectors mates. The puzzle is *assembled* when every clause piece snaps in.

Read it again and you will find a familiar object. A connector $(i, p)$ is a *literal*: "variable $i$ is true" when $p = 1$ and "variable $i$ is false" when $p = 0$. A clause piece is an OR of literals, and the whole puzzle is an AND of clauses. A framed jigsaw puzzle is a Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form, and an assembly is a satisfying assignment. Take the clauses $x_1 \lor x_2$ and $\lnot x_2 \lor x_3$. As a puzzle, the first clause piece has connectors (socket 1, tab) and (socket 2, tab). The second has (socket 2, blank) and (socket 3, tab). Out of the $2^3 = 8$ ways to fill the sockets, exactly four assemble the puzzle:
$$011,\quad 100,\quad 101,\quad 111 .$$

We call the number of assemblies the **assembly count** of the puzzle $P$ and write it $\#P$. (The symbol is chosen to echo the complexity class #P, which is about counting.)

## Deciding versus counting

Asking whether a puzzle can be assembled *at all* is exactly the satisfiability problem SAT, the original NP-complete problem. Asking *how many* assemblies exist is the counting problem #SAT. That problem is harder still. Leslie Valiant showed in 1979 that it is complete for #P, the class of problems that count the witnesses of an NP problem. Counting satisfying assignments is believed to be far beyond efficient computation, and the same goes for counting solutions to most combinatorial puzzles.

Between the yes/no question and the exact count sit the **modular counts**: the number of solutions modulo $2$, modulo $3$, or modulo any $k$. The parity question ("is the number of solutions odd?") defines a complexity class of its own, $\oplus$P, pronounced "parity-P". It is a strange class. Seinosuke Toda proved that a polynomial-time machine with access to $\#$P can decide anything in the whole polynomial hierarchy, and his proof goes through parity counting. Knowing *only the last bit* of a count can therefore be enormously informative.

This raises a design question. Suppose you want to move a counting question from one puzzle to another without disturbing it. You need a transformation that keeps not just the answer "solvable or not" but the exact number of solutions. Complexity theorists call such a map **parsimonious**: it is stingy and neither creates nor destroys witnesses. A parsimonious map preserves the count, so it automatically preserves the count modulo every $k$, including the parity.

## The flip

Here is the most natural transformation a puzzle maker could think of. Take a puzzle $P$ and **swap every tab for a blank and every blank for a tab** on every connector of every clause piece. Call the result the *complement* $\overline{P}$. In logical terms, every literal $x_i$ becomes $\lnot x_i$ and every $\lnot x_i$ becomes $x_i$.

The complement usually looks quite different. In our example $\overline{P}$ has the clauses $\lnot x_1 \lor \lnot x_2$ and $x_2 \lor \lnot x_3$, and its assemblies are
$$000,\quad 010,\quad 011,\quad 100 .$$
That is a different set, but it again has four elements. The reason is that each assembly of $\overline{P}$ is the bitwise complement of an assembly of $P$: $011 \leftrightarrow 100$, $100 \leftrightarrow 011$, $101 \leftrightarrow 010$, $111 \leftrightarrow 000$. If you flip the tabs on the clause pieces *and* flip the pieces in the sockets, every connection that used to mate still mates.

> **Complementation Theorem.** For every framed puzzle $P$, the puzzle and its complement have the same assembly count: $\#\overline{P} = \#P$. Flipping every variable piece is an explicit bijection between their assemblies. Consequently $\#\overline{P} \equiv \#P \pmod k$ for every modulus $k$. In particular, the puzzle has an odd number of assemblies exactly when its complement does.

The flip is also cheap. It changes one bit per connector, so it runs in linear time and produces a puzzle of exactly the same size. Doing it twice gives back the original puzzle. In the language of complexity theory, complementation is a size-preserving, involutive, **parsimonious self-reduction** of the assembly-counting problem. It is a free symmetry of the space of instances.

## The flip is one member of a larger family

The flip turns out to be one element of a much bigger symmetry group.

Nothing forces us to flip *every* socket. Choose a set of sockets, written as a mask $\mu \in \{0,1\}^n$, and swap tab and blank only at the sockets with $\mu_i = 1$, both on the connectors and on the variable pieces. The same argument applies: a mating connection stays mating. We can also *relabel* the sockets with a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1, \dots, n\}$, moving everything aimed at socket $i$ to socket $\sigma(i)$. That plainly changes nothing essential either.

Combining a relabelling with a mask gives a **signed permutation**. Signed permutations form a group of order $2^n \cdot n!$, the *hyperoctahedral group*. It is the symmetry group of the $n$-dimensional cube, the same group that permutes and reflects the coordinate axes. Global complementation is the single element "no relabelling, flip everything".

> **Hyperoctahedral Invariance Theorem.** Every signed permutation $g$ carries the assemblies of a puzzle $P$ bijectively onto the assemblies of the transformed puzzle $g \cdot P$. Hence $\#(g\cdot P) = \#P$. Moreover, transforming by $h$ and then by $g$ is the same as transforming by the product $gh$ in the hyperoctahedral group, so the puzzles reachable from $P$ form a genuine orbit of a group action, and the count is constant along that whole orbit.

There is a geometric way to see this. The assemblies of $P$ form a subset of the corners of the $n$-cube, and a signed permutation is a rigid symmetry of that cube. Transforming the puzzle moves its solution set by a symmetry of the cube. A symmetry of the cube cannot change how many corners a set contains.

## When the flip does nothing

Could the complement of a puzzle be the very same puzzle? Then the "self-reduction" would be trivial on that instance. This happens only in a degenerate case.

> **Freeness Theorem.** $\overline{P} = P$ if and only if every clause piece of $P$ has no connectors at all.

A single connector $(i, p)$ turns into $(i, 1 - p)$, which is different. So any puzzle with at least one connector moves when flipped. Apart from the degenerate puzzles, the instance space therefore splits into pairs $\{P, \overline{P}\}$ of distinct puzzles with equal counts.

## Symmetry forces divisibility by powers of two

The group action has a second, more arithmetic consequence. Some puzzles are fixed by part of the group. Consider the masks $\mu$ that map the *solution set* of $P$ onto itself: flipping the sockets selected by $\mu$ sends every assembly to another assembly. These masks form a subgroup $H_P$ of $\{0,1\}^n$ under bitwise XOR. Every subgroup of $\{0,1\}^n$ has size a power of two, say $|H_P| = 2^k$. A nonzero mask moves every string, so the group splits the solution set into orbits of exactly $2^k$ assemblies each.

> **2-adic Certificate Theorem.** For every puzzle $P$, the order $|H_P| = 2^k$ of its mask-symmetry group divides the assembly count $\#P$. This order is unchanged by every signed permutation. In particular, if $\#P$ is odd, the mask-symmetry group of $P$ is trivial.

A puzzle with a visible flip symmetry therefore has an even number of solutions. Its parity is determined before any counting starts. In random experiments on small puzzles, the power of two dividing the count very often equals $2^k$ exactly, so the symmetry tends to explain *all* of the 2-adic structure of the count.

## Counting parity without counting

How would one compute the parity of $\#P$ directly? Use the classic inclusion–exclusion principle. For a set $S$ of clause pieces, let $F_S$ be the set of fillings that make **every** piece in $S$ fail. Then
$$\#P \;=\; \sum_{S \subseteq \text{clauses}} (-1)^{|S|}\, |F_S| .$$
Modulo $2$ the signs disappear, because $-1 \equiv 1$, which leaves
$$\#P \;\equiv\; \sum_{S} |F_S| \pmod 2 .$$
Each $F_S$ also has a simple shape. Making a clause piece fail means *every* connector $(i, p)$ on it must fail, so socket $i$ is forced to hold $1 - p$. Each failure set is therefore either empty (if two of the forced values conflict) or a subcube of dimension $n - (\text{number of sockets forced})$, with $2^{n - (\text{number of sockets forced})}$ elements. That number is odd only when it equals $1$. The parity of the count is the parity of the number of clause subsets that are *consistent* and *pin down every single socket*. In our example no subset pins all three sockets, and indeed $\#P = 4$ is even.

## Where parsimony actually breaks

If the mathematics preserves counts so faithfully, where does counting information get lost? The answer is in the physical pieces.

A real jigsaw has physical pieces, and some of those pieces are interchangeable. When a framed puzzle with $m$ clause pieces is turned into a pile of labelled physical pieces, swapping interchangeable pieces gives new "labelled" assemblies that are mathematically the same solution. Their number is
$$\#_{\text{labelled}}(P) \;=\; \#P \cdot (m+2)! \cdot n! \cdot n! .$$

> **Encoding Theorem.** The labelled assembly count is always even. For any solvable puzzle it differs from $\#P$, so the physical encoding is never parsimonious on solvable instances. It still preserves solvability, because the labelled count is zero exactly when $\#P$ is zero.

So the encoding destroys exactly the information that complementation keeps. It preserves the yes/no answer but wipes out the parity: every labelled count is even, whatever $\#P$ is. The factorials record the multiplicities of interchangeable pieces. **Piece multiplicities carry counting information**, and the mathematics of complementation does not lose it. The physical packaging does.

## Hardness is inherited, not lost

Finally, the logical translation in both directions is parsimonious. A DIMACS-style CNF formula becomes a puzzle with the same number of solutions, and a puzzle becomes a formula with the same number of solutions. Composing parsimonious maps gives a parsimonious map. So any counting problem that reduces parsimoniously to #SAT also reduces parsimoniously to jigsaw assembly counting, and that reduction preserves every modular count. Combined with Valiant's theorem, exact assembly counting is as hard as #SAT. Parity counting for jigsaws inherits all the hardness of parity counting for SAT, and the same holds for every other modulus.

The overall picture is easy to state. The space of jigsaw instances has a large free symmetry, the hyperoctahedral group, and that symmetry preserves exact counts and therefore all modular counts. Counting stays hard anyway: the symmetry gives no shortcut to the count. What it does supply is a source of easy *divisibility* information, namely powers of two forced by self-symmetry. Separately, the physical encoding, not the mathematics, throws away the parity.

## What's next

Several questions remain open. A Burnside-type sum over signed cycle types should count the essentially different two-clause puzzles, meaning the orbits of the hyperoctahedral group. It is natural to ask exactly when the 2-adic certificate from symmetry is sharp. And the parity criterion through fully pinning clause subsets invites a search for structured families of puzzles whose parity becomes easy.

So the next time you assemble a jigsaw, imagine turning every tab inside out. The finished picture would be a different one, but the number of ways to finish it would stay exactly the same.

# Parity-Preserving Self-Reduction for Jigsaw Assembly Counting

**Aristotle**

*October 2026*

---

## Abstract

We study the problem of counting the assemblies of *framed jigsaw puzzles*. In this combinatorial model, $n$ variable sockets each receive a tab or a blank piece, and clause pieces snap into place when at least one of their connectors mates. The model is literally conjunctive normal form, so the assembly count of a puzzle equals the number of satisfying assignments of a CNF formula. Our main structural result concerns the hyperoctahedral group $B_n = (\mathbb{Z}/2)^n \rtimes S_n$ of signed permutations of the sockets. This group acts on puzzles through a genuine group action, and each group element induces an explicit bijection between the assembly spaces of $P$ and $g\cdot P$. The assembly count is therefore an orbit invariant. Global tab/blank complementation $P \mapsto \overline{P}$ is the special element $(\mathrm{id}, \mathbf 1)$. It is a size-preserving, involutive, linear-time **parsimonious self-reduction** of assembly counting, so it preserves the count modulo every integer $k$, in particular the parity. Complementation acts freely on the instance space apart from the degenerate puzzles whose clause pieces are all empty. Translations of the cube that stabilise the solution set give *2-adic certificates*: the order $2^k$ of this mask-symmetry group divides the count, it is a $B_n$-invariant, and odd counts force it to be trivial. We give the mod-2 count by signless inclusion–exclusion over clause subsets. A short argument reduces this to counting clause subsets that consistently pin every socket. We show that the translations between DIMACS CNF and puzzles are parsimonious in both directions, so every modular-counting hardness result for SAT transfers to jigsaw assembly. Finally, we show that the physical encoding into labelled pieces multiplies the count by $(m+2)!\,(n!)^2$. That encoding is never parsimonious on solvable instances and always produces an even count. The loss of counting information therefore comes from the encoding and not from the underlying mathematics.

---

## 1. Introduction

Reductions between combinatorial problems usually preserve only *solvability*. A reduction $f$ from a decision problem $A$ to a decision problem $B$ only needs $x \in A \iff f(x)\in B$. Counting complexity asks for more. A reduction is **parsimonious** when the number of witnesses of $f(x)$ equals the number of witnesses of $x$. Parsimonious reductions are the natural morphisms of the class $\#\mathrm{P}$ introduced by Valiant (1979). Since a parsimonious reduction preserves the exact count, it also preserves the count modulo every $k$. So it transports hardness for every modular counting class $\mathrm{Mod}_k\mathrm{P}$ at once, including $\oplus\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{Mod}_2\mathrm{P}$.

Jigsaw puzzles are a classical source of NP-complete problems. This paper studies a framed variant in which the frame contributes $n$ binary *variable sockets* and the remaining pieces act as *clauses*. The variant is designed so that solving it is exactly satisfiability. The question we address is how the natural symmetries of the instance space interact with counting. The most natural symmetry is global complementation: swap every tab for a blank and vice versa. This map is a bijection on instances, and we ask whether it is also a bijection on *witnesses*. If it is, it is a parsimonious self-reduction, and every modular count is a complementation invariant.

We show that this is the case, and more. Complementation is one element of a parsimonious action of the full hyperoctahedral group. The action has three consequences:

1. **Invariance.** The exact count is constant on orbits (Theorems 3.3 and 3.5), and hence so is every modular count (Corollary 4.2).
2. **Freeness.** Complementation fixes no instance except the degenerate ones (Theorem 4.3).
3. **Divisibility.** Stabilisers in the translation subgroup produce powers of two dividing the count (Theorem 5.2).

We also describe exactly where parsimony fails: in the physical encoding by labelled pieces (Theorem 7.3), not in the mathematics.

**Scope.** The model of efficiency used here is the encoding-size bound: every reduction we construct produces an output whose size is at most linear in the input size. All of these maps are evidently computable in linear time. We do not reprove that #SAT is #P-complete. We use the classical fact as a black box and prove the parsimonious transfer from #SAT to jigsaw counting.

---

## 2. The model

Throughout, $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2$ and $[n] = \{1,\dots,n\}$. We write the Boolean cube additively:
$$Q_n = \mathbb{F}_2^{\,n}, \qquad a = (a_1,\dots,a_n).$$
A coordinate $a_i = 1$ means socket $i$ holds the tab piece, and $a_i = 0$ means it holds the blank.

**Definition 2.1 (Literal input, clause piece, framed puzzle).** A *literal input* on $n$ sockets is a pair $\ell = (i,p) \in [n]\times\mathbb{F}_2$: a socket together with the polarity it is milled for. A *clause piece* is a finite list of literal inputs. A *framed puzzle* $P$ on $n$ sockets is a finite list $P = (c_1,\dots,c_m)$ of clause pieces. Its *size* is $|P| = m + \sum_j |c_j|$.

**Definition 2.2 (Fitting, assembling).** A literal input $(i,p)$ *fits* a filling $a\in Q_n$ when $a_i = p$. A filling $a$ *assembles* $P$ when every clause piece contains a literal input that fits:
$$a \models P \quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall c\in P\;\; \exists (i,p)\in c:\; a_i = p.$$
The *assembly space* is $\mathcal{A}(P) = \{a\in Q_n : a\models P\}$, and the *assembly count* is $\#P = |\mathcal{A}(P)|$.

A literal $(i,1)$ is the positive literal $x_i$ and $(i,0)$ is the negative literal $\lnot x_i$. Under this dictionary a puzzle is a CNF formula, $a \models P$ is satisfaction, and $\#P$ is the number of satisfying assignments. A clause piece with no inputs can never snap in, so a puzzle containing one has $\#P = 0$. The empty puzzle has $\#P = 2^n$.

**Example 2.3.** Let $n=3$ and $P = \big((1,1),(2,1)\big),\big((2,0),(3,1)\big)$, i.e. $(x_1\lor x_2)\land(\lnot x_2\lor x_3)$. Then $\mathcal{A}(P) = \{011, 100, 101, 111\}$ (written $a_1a_2a_3$) and $\#P = 4$.

---

## 3. The hyperoctahedral action

**Definition 3.1 (Signed permutation).** A *signed permutation* of the sockets is a pair $g = (\sigma,\mu)$ with $\sigma\in S_n$ and $\mu\in Q_n$. It acts on literal inputs, puzzles and fillings by
$$g\cdot(i,p) = \big(\sigma(i),\; p + \mu_i\big), \qquad g\cdot P = \big(\,(g\cdot\ell)_{\ell\in c}\,\big)_{c\in P},$$
$$(g\cdot a)_j = a_{\sigma^{-1}(j)} + \mu_{\sigma^{-1}(j)}.$$
That is, socket $i$ is relabelled $\sigma(i)$, and the tab/blank polarity at socket $i$ is flipped exactly when $\mu_i = 1$. The inverse action on fillings is $(g^{-1}\cdot b)_i = b_{\sigma(i)} - \mu_i$. It satisfies $g^{-1}\cdot(g\cdot a) = a$ and $g\cdot(g^{-1}\cdot b)=b$, so $a\mapsto g\cdot a$ is a bijection of $Q_n$.

**Lemma 3.2 (Literal-level transport).** For every $g$, $a$ and $\ell$: $\;g\cdot\ell$ fits $g\cdot a$ $\iff$ $\ell$ fits $a$.

*Proof.* Let $\ell=(i,p)$. Then $(g\cdot a)_{\sigma(i)} = a_i + \mu_i$ and $g\cdot \ell = (\sigma(i), p+\mu_i)$. So the condition reads $a_i+\mu_i = p+\mu_i$, which is equivalent to $a_i = p$ by cancellation in $\mathbb{F}_2$. $\square$

**Theorem 3.3 (Witness-preserving bijection).** For every signed permutation $g$ and every puzzle $P$, and for every filling $a$,
$$g\cdot a \models g\cdot P \iff a\models P.$$
Consequently $a\mapsto g\cdot a$ restricts to a bijection $\mathcal{A}(P)\to\mathcal{A}(g\cdot P)$ with inverse $b\mapsto g^{-1}\cdot b$. Equivalently, $\mathcal{A}(g\cdot P) = g\cdot\mathcal{A}(P)$, and in particular
$$\#(g\cdot P) = \#P.$$

*Proof.* The clause pieces of $g\cdot P$ are the images $g\cdot c$ of the clause pieces $c$ of $P$, and the inputs of $g\cdot c$ are the images of the inputs of $c$. Suppose $a \models P$, and take a clause piece $g\cdot c$. Choose an input $\ell \in c$ that fits $a$. By Lemma 3.2, $g\cdot\ell$ fits $g\cdot a$. Conversely, suppose $g\cdot a\models g\cdot P$ and take $c\in P$. Some input of $g\cdot c$ fits $g\cdot a$. That input has the form $g\cdot\ell$ with $\ell\in c$, and Lemma 3.2 shows $\ell$ fits $a$. The two maps on fillings are mutually inverse, so the restriction is a bijection. $\square$

**Definition 3.4 (Group law).** Define $g h = (\sigma_g\sigma_h,\; \nu)$ with $\nu_i = \mu_{h,i} + \mu_{g,\sigma_h(i)}$. The product means "first $h$, then $g$". This is the multiplication of the wreath product $\mathbb{F}_2\wr S_n = B_n$, a group of order $2^n n!$.

**Theorem 3.5 (Action compatibility and orbit invariance).** For all $g,h$ and $P$, $(gh)\cdot P = g\cdot(h\cdot P)$. Consequently, for any finite word $g_1g_2\cdots g_r$,
$$\#\big(g_1\cdot(g_2\cdot(\cdots(g_r\cdot P)\cdots))\big) = \#P,$$
so the assembly count is constant on every $B_n$-orbit of puzzles.

*Proof.* It suffices to check the identity on literal inputs:
$$g\cdot(h\cdot(i,p)) = g\cdot(\sigma_h(i),\,p+\mu_{h,i}) = (\sigma_g\sigma_h(i),\; p+\mu_{h,i}+\mu_{g,\sigma_h(i)}) = (gh)\cdot(i,p).$$
Mapping over clause pieces and over the puzzle preserves this identity. Orbit invariance then follows by induction on the length of the word, using Theorem 3.3 at each step. $\square$

**Remark 3.6 (Geometry).** $B_n$ is the symmetry group of the $n$-cube, and $a\mapsto g\cdot a$ is the corresponding isometry of $Q_n$ for the Hamming metric. Theorem 3.3 says that transforming the instance moves the solution set by a cube symmetry. Every invariant of subsets of $Q_n$ under cube symmetries is therefore an invariant of puzzles. This includes cardinality, the weight enumerator up to complementation, and the dimension of the affine hull.

---

## 4. Complementation as a parsimonious self-reduction

**Definition 4.1 (Complement).** The *complement* of $P$ is $\overline{P} = (\mathrm{id},\mathbf{1})\cdot P$, obtained by replacing every input $(i,p)$ with $(i,p+1)$. On fillings, $(\mathrm{id},\mathbf 1)$ acts by bitwise negation $a\mapsto a+\mathbf 1$.

**Corollary 4.2 (Complementation is parsimonious).** For every puzzle $P$:

1. $a\models P \iff a+\mathbf{1}\models\overline{P}$, so bitwise negation is an explicit bijection $\mathcal{A}(P)\to\mathcal{A}(\overline{P})$;
2. $\#\overline{P} = \#P$;
3. $\#\overline{P}\equiv\#P \pmod k$ for every $k\ge 1$. In particular, $\#P$ is even if and only if $\#\overline P$ is even;
4. $\overline{\overline{P}} = P$ and $|\overline{P}| = |P|$.

*Proof.* Items 1–3 are Theorem 3.3 applied to $g = (\mathrm{id},\mathbf 1)$. Item 4 holds because $p+1+1 = p$ in $\mathbb{F}_2$ and the shape of the list of lists is unchanged. $\square$

In the language of reductions, define a **counting problem** to be a set of instances $X$ with a size function $|\cdot|$ and a count $c_X : X\to\mathbb{N}$. A **parsimonious reduction** from $(X,c_X)$ to $(Y,c_Y)$ is a map $f:X\to Y$ with $c_Y(f(x)) = c_X(x)$ and $|f(x)| \le C|x| + D$ for constants $C, D$. Corollary 4.2 shows that complementation is a parsimonious self-reduction of $\#\mathrm{Jigsaw} = (\text{puzzles},\#)$ with $C=1$, $D=0$. It is computable in a single linear pass.

**Theorem 4.3 (Freeness).** $\overline{P} = P$ if and only if every clause piece of $P$ is empty.

*Proof.* If all clause pieces are empty there is nothing to flip. Conversely, $\overline{P}$ has the same shape as $P$. If some clause piece has an input $(i,p)$, then the corresponding position of $\overline P$ holds $(i,p+1)\ne(i,p)$. $\square$

Thus $\langle(\mathrm{id},\mathbf 1)\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ acts freely on the non-degenerate puzzles. That part of the instance space is partitioned into pairs $\{P,\overline P\}$ of distinct instances with equal counts. Degenerate puzzles have count $0$ if they contain at least one (empty) clause and count $2^n$ if they have no clauses.

---

## 5. Mask symmetries and 2-adic certificates

The translations $\tau_\mu = (\mathrm{id},\mu)$ form the normal subgroup $\mathbb{F}_2^{\,n}\trianglelefteq B_n$.

**Definition 5.1 (Mask-symmetry group).** For a puzzle $P$ let
$$H_P = \{\mu\in Q_n : \mathcal{A}(P) + \mu = \mathcal{A}(P)\},$$
the stabiliser of the assembly space under translations. It is a subgroup of $Q_n$, i.e. an $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear subspace. Every mask $\mu$ with $\tau_\mu\cdot P = P$, or more generally with $\tau_\mu\cdot P$ having the same assembly space as $P$, lies in $H_P$ by Theorem 3.3, so the results below apply to those masks as well.

**Theorem 5.2 (2-adic certificate).** For every puzzle $P$:

1. $|H_P| = 2^k$ with $k = \dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}H_P$, and $2^k$ divides $\#P$. In fact $\#P = 2^k\cdot\big|\mathcal{A}(P)/H_P\big|$;
2. $|H_{g\cdot P}| = |H_P|$ for every signed permutation $g$;
3. if $\#P$ is odd, then $H_P = \{0\}$.

*Proof.* (1) $H_P$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^{\,n}$, so its order is a power of two. It acts on the finite set $\mathcal{A}(P)$ by translation, and the action is free because $a+\mu = a$ forces $\mu = 0$. All orbits therefore have size $|H_P|$, and $|\mathcal{A}(P)| = |H_P|\cdot\#\text{orbits}$. (2) Write $g = (\sigma,\mu_g)$. A direct computation gives $g\cdot(a+\nu) = g\cdot a + \nu\circ\sigma^{-1}$, i.e. $g\tau_\nu g^{-1} = \tau_{\nu\circ\sigma^{-1}}$. Combined with $\mathcal{A}(g\cdot P) = g\cdot\mathcal{A}(P)$ (Theorem 3.3), this yields $H_{g\cdot P} = \{\nu\circ\sigma^{-1} : \nu\in H_P\}$, which has the same order. (3) If $2^k$ divides an odd number then $k=0$. $\square$

The certificate is cheap to state and often sharp. Let $v_2$ denote the 2-adic valuation. On random puzzles with $n\le 4$ sockets, $v_2(\#P) = k$ held for the large majority of solvable samples (242 of 243 in the experiment reported in Section 8). By part (1), the gap $v_2(\#P)-k$ is exactly $v_2$ of the number of $H_P$-orbits on the assembly space.

---

## 6. The parity of the count

**Theorem 6.1 (Mod-2 count by signless inclusion–exclusion).** For a set $S$ of clause pieces of $P$, let $F_S = \{a\in Q_n : \text{no } c\in S \text{ has an input fitting } a\}$ be the set of common falsifiers. Then
$$\#P \equiv \sum_{S\subseteq P} |F_S| \pmod 2.$$

*Proof.* By inclusion–exclusion over the "bad" events "clause $c$ fails", $\#P = \sum_{S}(-1)^{|S|}|F_S|$. Reducing modulo $2$ removes the signs, since $-1\equiv 1$. $\square$

**Proposition 6.2 (Affine-subcube criterion).** Each $F_S$ is either empty or an affine subcube of $Q_n$. Call $S$ *consistent* if no socket is forced to both values, and *fully pinning* if every socket $i\in[n]$ occurs in some input of some clause in $S$. Then
$$\#P \equiv \big|\{S\subseteq P : S \text{ consistent and fully pinning}\}\big| \pmod 2.$$

*Proof.* A clause piece $c$ fails at $a$ exactly when $a_i = p+1$ for every input $(i,p)\in c$. So $F_S$ is the set of fillings satisfying the pinning constraints $\{a_i = p+1 : (i,p)\in c\in S\}$. If two constraints conflict, $F_S=\varnothing$. Otherwise the pinned sockets $V(S)$ are fixed and the rest are free, so $|F_S| = 2^{\,n-|V(S)|}$. This number is odd exactly when $V(S) = [n]$. Substituting into Theorem 6.1 gives the claim. $\square$

In Example 2.3 the falsifier sizes are $|F_\varnothing| = 8$, $|F_{\{c_1\}}| = |F_{\{c_2\}}| = 2$ and $|F_{\{c_1,c_2\}}| = 0$. No subset is fully pinning, and indeed $\#P = 8-2-2+0 = 4$ is even.

Proposition 6.2 is a sum over $2^m$ subsets. It does not make parity counting easy in general, which is consistent with $\oplus\mathrm{SAT}$ being $\oplus\mathrm{P}$-complete. It does show that only clause subsets with at least $n$ distinct sockets can contribute. It also identifies combinatorial families (for instance, puzzles in which no subset of clause pieces covers all sockets consistently) where the parity is forced to be even.

---

## 7. Encodings: where parsimony breaks

### 7.1 SAT and jigsaw reduce to each other parsimoniously

A DIMACS CNF on variables $1,\dots,n$ is a list of clauses, each a list of nonzero integers. Translate the literal $+v$ to $(v,1)$ and $-v$ to $(v,0)$. This gives a puzzle on $n$ sockets with the same shape. The reverse translation inverts it.

**Theorem 7.1 (Two-way parsimony).** The translations $\mathrm{CNF}\to\mathrm{Puzzle}$ and $\mathrm{Puzzle}\to\mathrm{CNF}$ are mutually inverse, size-preserving and parsimonious: the number of satisfying assignments of the formula equals the assembly count of the puzzle.

**Corollary 7.2 (Hardness transfer).** If a counting problem $(X,c_X)$ reduces parsimoniously to $\#\mathrm{SAT}$, then it reduces parsimoniously to $\#\mathrm{Jigsaw}$. Hence for every $k$ it also reduces to the problem of computing $\#P \bmod k$. Since #SAT is #P-complete under parsimonious reductions (Valiant), exact jigsaw assembly counting is #P-complete, and computing $\#P\bmod k$ is $\mathrm{Mod}_k\mathrm{P}$-hard.

*Proof.* Composition of parsimonious maps is parsimonious, and linear size bounds compose to linear size bounds. $\square$

### 7.2 Labelled physical assemblies

To build a physical jigsaw, a framed puzzle with $m$ clause pieces on $n$ sockets is encoded as a pile of labelled pieces. Some of those pieces are physically interchangeable; the multiplicity factor below records the relabellings of interchangeable pieces (one family of size $m+2$ and two families of size $n$). A *labelled assembly* records which physical piece sits where. Each mathematical assembly therefore lifts to many labelled ones.

**Theorem 7.3 (The encoding breaks parsimony).** The number of labelled physical assemblies is
$$\#_{\mathrm{lab}}(P) = \#P\cdot(m+2)!\cdot n!\cdot n!.$$
Consequently:

1. $\#_{\mathrm{lab}}(P)$ is always even;
2. $\#_{\mathrm{lab}}(P) = 0\iff\#P = 0$, so the encoding is a valid *decision* reduction;
3. if $\#P>0$ then $\#_{\mathrm{lab}}(P)\ne\#P$, so the encoding is never parsimonious on a solvable instance.

*Proof.* Each mathematical assembly lifts to exactly $(m+2)!\,(n!)^2$ labelled ones, one for each way of distributing the interchangeable labels. Since $(m+2)!\ge 2$, the product is even and is strictly larger than $\#P$ whenever $\#P\ge 1$. $\square$

Corollary 4.2 and Theorem 7.3 show where counting information goes. The symmetry $P\mapsto\overline P$ preserves all of it. The physical encoding keeps the zero/nonzero distinction and erases the parity entirely: the multiplicity factor $(m+2)!(n!)^2$ is even, so $\#_{\mathrm{lab}}\equiv 0\pmod 2$ for every puzzle. **Piece multiplicities carry counting information.** A counting-faithful physical encoding would have to break the interchangeability, for example by making every piece unique, or would have to divide out the known multiplicity.

---

## 8. Algorithms and experiments

**Algorithm A (brute-force assembly count).** Enumerate $a\in Q_n$ and test $a\models P$ in time $O(|P|)$ per filling. Total cost: $O(2^n|P|)$.

**Algorithm B (witness transport).** Given $g=(\sigma,\mu)$ and $a\in\mathcal A(P)$, output $g\cdot a$ in $O(n)$ time. Theorem 3.3 guarantees that the output lies in $\mathcal A(g\cdot P)$. Transforming the instance costs $O(|P|)$.

**Algorithm C (parity by pinning).** For each $S\subseteq P$, maintain a partial assignment of forced values $a_i=p+1$. Abort on conflict, and count $S$ if all $n$ sockets end up forced. Cost: $O(2^m|P|)$. This is preferable to Algorithm A when $m < n$.

**Algorithm D (mask-symmetry group).** For each $\mu\in Q_n$, test whether $\mathcal A(P)+\mu = \mathcal A(P)$. Cost: $O(2^n\,\#P)$ after computing $\mathcal A(P)$.

We implemented all four algorithms and tested the results above on enumerated and random instances:

- Theorem 3.3 on 1440 random (puzzle, signed permutation) pairs with $n\le 4$, checking that $g\cdot\mathcal A(P) = \mathcal A(g\cdot P)$.
- Theorem 3.5 on 300 random triples $(g,h,P)$.
- Corollary 4.2 and Theorem 4.3 *exhaustively* on all two-clause puzzles with clause width at most $2$, for $n=1,2,3$ (16, 121 and 484 puzzles). This covered counts modulo $2,3,5$, involutivity, size preservation and the freeness criterion.
- Theorem 5.2 on 400 random puzzles, including the $B_n$-invariance of $|H_P|$.
- Theorem 6.1 and Proposition 6.2 on 300 random puzzles. The three parity computations agreed in every case.
- Theorem 7.1 on 200 random CNFs.

For Example 2.3 with $m=2$, $n=3$, the labelled count is $4\cdot 4!\cdot 3!\cdot 3! = 3456$, while $\#P = 4$.

---

## 9. Discussion

Complementation was conjectured to be a parsimonious self-reduction, making the mod-2 count a complementation invariant while the exact count stays #P-hard. This holds, for a structural reason: the full hyperoctahedral group acts on instances and on witnesses compatibly. Such a symmetry does not make counting easier. The orbit of $P$ has at most $2^n n!$ elements, all with the same count, and the count of any one of them is still #P-hard to compute. What the symmetry does give is (i) free equivalences between instances, useful for canonicalisation and for symmetry breaking in model counters, and (ii) arithmetic information about stabilisers, in the form of the powers of two in Theorem 5.2.

The negative result of Theorem 7.3 is equally informative. Standard NP-hardness reductions for physical puzzles are not counting-faithful, because physically identical pieces generate labelled solutions in multiplicity. The multiplicity factor here is a product of factorials. That factor is divisible by every prime $\le m+2$, so the encoding erases not only the parity but every $\mathrm{Mod}_q$ count for primes $q\le m+2$.

## 10. Future work

1. **Burnside census.** $B_n$ genuinely acts on puzzles (Theorem 3.5), so Burnside's lemma counts the orbits of two-clause puzzles on $n$ sockets as a sum over signed cycle types. Both $\#P$ and $|H_P|$ are constant on each orbit.
2. **Sharpness of the 2-adic certificate.** Characterise the puzzles with $v_2(\#P) = \log_2|H_P|$, i.e. those for which the number of $H_P$-orbits on $\mathcal{A}(P)$ is odd. Prove that this is the generic case for small $n$.
3. **Parity-tractable families.** Use Proposition 6.2 to identify structural classes, for example puzzles whose clause hypergraph cannot be covered consistently, in which the parity is computable in polynomial time.
4. **Counting-faithful encodings.** Design physical encodings whose multiplicity factor is a known odd number, or is $1$, so that modular counts survive the passage to real pieces.

\section{Introduction}

Reductions between combinatorial problems usually preserve only
\emph{solvability}. A reduction $f$ from a decision problem $A$ to a decision
problem $B$ only needs $x\in A\iff f(x)\in B$. Counting complexity asks for more.
A reduction is \emph{parsimonious} when the number of witnesses of $f(x)$ equals
the number of witnesses of $x$. Parsimonious reductions are the natural morphisms
of the class $\#\mathrm{P}$ introduced by Valiant. Since a parsimonious reduction
preserves the exact count, it also preserves the count modulo every $k$. So it
transports hardness for every modular counting class $\mathrm{Mod}_k\mathrm{P}$
at once, including $\oplus\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{Mod}_2\mathrm{P}$.

Jigsaw puzzles are a classical source of NP-complete problems. This paper studies
a framed variant in which the frame contributes $n$ binary \emph{variable sockets}
and the remaining pieces act as \emph{clauses}. The variant is designed so that
solving it is exactly satisfiability. The question we address is how the natural
symmetries of the instance space interact with counting. The most natural
symmetry is global complementation: swap every tab for a blank and vice versa.
This map is a bijection on instances, and we ask whether it is also a bijection
on \emph{witnesses}. If it is, it is a parsimonious self-reduction, and every
modular count is a complementation invariant.

We show that this is the case, and more. Complementation is one element of a
parsimonious action of the full hyperoctahedral group. The action has three
consequences:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Invariance.} The exact count is constant on orbits
  (Theorems~\ref{thm:bij} and~\ref{thm:action}), and hence so is every modular
  count (Corollary~\ref{cor:comp}).
\item \textbf{Freeness.} Complementation fixes no instance except the degenerate
  ones (Theorem~\ref{thm:free}).
\item \textbf{Divisibility.} Stabilisers in the translation subgroup produce
  powers of two dividing the count (Theorem~\ref{thm:2adic}).
\end{enumerate}
We also describe exactly where parsimony fails: in the physical encoding by
labelled pieces (Theorem~\ref{thm:enc}), not in the mathematics.

\emph{Scope.} The model of efficiency used here is the encoding-size bound: every
reduction we construct produces an output whose size is at most linear in the
input size. All of these maps are evidently computable in linear time. We do not
reprove that $\#$SAT is $\#$P-complete. We use the classical fact as a black box
and prove the parsimonious transfer from $\#$SAT to jigsaw counting.

\section{The model}

Throughout, $\F=\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$. We write the Boolean cube
additively: $Q_n=\F^{\,n}$. A coordinate $a_i=1$ means socket $i$ holds the tab
piece, and $a_i=0$ means it holds the blank.

\begin{definition}[Literal input, clause piece, framed puzzle]
A \emph{literal input} on $n$ sockets is a pair $\ell=(i,p)\in[n]\times\F$: a
socket together with the polarity it is milled for. A \emph{clause piece} is a
finite list of literal inputs. A \emph{framed puzzle} $P$ on $n$ sockets is a
finite list $P=(c_1,\dots,c_m)$ of clause pieces. Its \emph{size} is
$|P|=m+\sum_j|c_j|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fitting, assembling]
A literal input $(i,p)$ \emph{fits} a filling $a\in Q_n$ when $a_i=p$. A filling
$a$ \emph{assembles} $P$, written $a\models P$, when every clause piece contains a
literal input that fits:
\[
a\models P\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall c\in P\ \exists(i,p)\in c:\ a_i=p .
\]
The \emph{assembly space} is $\A(P)=\{a\in Q_n: a\models P\}$, and the
\emph{assembly count} is $\#P=|\A(P)|$.
\end{definition}

A literal $(i,1)$ is the positive literal $x_i$ and $(i,0)$ is the negative
literal $\lnot x_i$. Under this dictionary a puzzle is a CNF formula,
$a\models P$ is satisfaction, and $\#P$ is the number of satisfying assignments.
A clause piece with no inputs can never snap in, so a puzzle containing one has
$\#P=0$. The empty puzzle has $\#P=2^n$.

\begin{example}\label{ex:main}
Let $n=3$ and $P=\big((1,1),(2,1)\big),\big((2,0),(3,1)\big)$, i.e.\
$(x_1\lor x_2)\land(\lnot x_2\lor x_3)$. Then
$\A(P)=\{011,100,101,111\}$ (written $a_1a_2a_3$) and $\#P=4$.
\end{example}

\section{The hyperoctahedral action}

\begin{definition}[Signed permutation]
A \emph{signed permutation} is a pair $g=(\sigma,\mu)$ with $\sigma\in S_n$ and
$\mu\in Q_n$. It acts on literal inputs, puzzles and fillings by
\[
g\cdot(i,p)=(\sigma(i),\,p+\mu_i),\qquad
g\cdot P=\big((g\cdot\ell)_{\ell\in c}\big)_{c\in P},\qquad
(g\cdot a)_j=a_{\sigma^{-1}(j)}+\mu_{\sigma^{-1}(j)} .
\]
That is, socket $i$ is relabelled $\sigma(i)$, and the polarity at socket $i$ is
flipped exactly when $\mu_i=1$. The inverse action on fillings is
$(g^{-1}\cdot b)_i=b_{\sigma(i)}-\mu_i$. It satisfies
$g^{-1}\cdot(g\cdot a)=a$ and $g\cdot(g^{-1}\cdot b)=b$, so $a\mapsto g\cdot a$ is
a bijection of $Q_n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Literal-level transport]\label{lem:lit}
For all $g$, $a$ and $\ell$: $g\cdot\ell$ fits $g\cdot a$ if and only if $\ell$
fits $a$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $\ell=(i,p)$. Then $(g\cdot a)_{\sigma(i)}=a_i+\mu_i$ and
$g\cdot\ell=(\sigma(i),p+\mu_i)$. So the condition reads $a_i+\mu_i=p+\mu_i$,
which is equivalent to $a_i=p$ by cancellation in $\F$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Witness-preserving bijection]\label{thm:bij}
For every signed permutation $g$, every puzzle $P$ and every filling $a$,
$g\cdot a\models g\cdot P\iff a\models P$. Consequently $a\mapsto g\cdot a$
restricts to a bijection $\A(P)\to\A(g\cdot P)$ with inverse
$b\mapsto g^{-1}\cdot b$. Equivalently $\A(g\cdot P)=g\cdot\A(P)$, and in
particular $\#(g\cdot P)=\#P$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The clause pieces of $g\cdot P$ are the images $g\cdot c$ of the clause pieces
$c$ of $P$, and the inputs of $g\cdot c$ are the images of the inputs of $c$.
Suppose $a\models P$, and take a clause piece $g\cdot c$. Choose an input
$\ell\in c$ that fits $a$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:lit}, $g\cdot\ell$ fits $g\cdot a$.
Conversely, suppose $g\cdot a\models g\cdot P$ and take $c\in P$. Some input of
$g\cdot c$ fits $g\cdot a$. That input has the form $g\cdot\ell$ with $\ell\in c$,
and Lemma~\ref{lem:lit} shows $\ell$ fits $a$. The two maps on fillings are
mutually inverse, so the restriction is a bijection.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Group law]
Define $gh=(\sigma_g\sigma_h,\nu)$ with $\nu_i=\mu_{h,i}+\mu_{g,\sigma_h(i)}$. The
product means ``first $h$, then $g$''. This is the multiplication of the wreath
product $\F\wr S_n=B_n$, a group of order $2^n n!$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Action compatibility and orbit invariance]\label{thm:action}
For all $g,h$ and $P$, $(gh)\cdot P=g\cdot(h\cdot P)$. Consequently, for any
finite word $g_1\cdots g_r$ of signed permutations,
$\#\big(g_1\cdot(g_2\cdot(\cdots(g_r\cdot P)\cdots))\big)=\#P$, so the assembly
count is constant on every $B_n$-orbit.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
On literal inputs,
$g\cdot(h\cdot(i,p))=(\sigma_g\sigma_h(i),\,p+\mu_{h,i}+\mu_{g,\sigma_h(i)})=(gh)\cdot(i,p)$.
Mapping over clause pieces and over the puzzle preserves this identity. Orbit
invariance follows by induction on the length of the word, using
Theorem~\ref{thm:bij} at each step.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
$B_n$ is the symmetry group of the $n$-cube, and $a\mapsto g\cdot a$ is the
corresponding Hamming isometry of $Q_n$. Theorem~\ref{thm:bij} says that
transforming the instance moves the solution set by a cube symmetry. Every
invariant of subsets of $Q_n$ under cube symmetries is therefore an invariant of
puzzles.
\end{remark}

\section{Complementation as a parsimonious self-reduction}

\begin{definition}[Complement]
The \emph{complement} of $P$ is $\comp P=(\mathrm{id},\mathbf 1)\cdot P$,
obtained by replacing every input $(i,p)$ with $(i,p+1)$. On fillings,
$(\mathrm{id},\mathbf 1)$ acts by bitwise negation $a\mapsto a+\mathbf 1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[Complementation is parsimonious]\label{cor:comp}
For every puzzle $P$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $a\models P\iff a+\mathbf 1\models\comp P$, so bitwise negation is an
  explicit bijection $\A(P)\to\A(\comp P)$;
\item $\#\comp P=\#P$;
\item $\#\comp P\equiv\#P\pmod k$ for every $k\ge1$; in particular $\#P$ is even
  if and only if $\#\comp P$ is even;
\item $\comp{\comp P}=P$ and $|\comp P|=|P|$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Items (1)--(3) are Theorem~\ref{thm:bij} with $g=(\mathrm{id},\mathbf 1)$. Item
(4) holds because $p+1+1=p$ in $\F$ and the shape is unchanged.
\end{proof}

A \emph{counting problem} is a set of instances $X$ with a size function and a
count $c_X:X\to\mathbb N$. A \emph{parsimonious reduction} from $(X,c_X)$ to
$(Y,c_Y)$ is a map $f:X\to Y$ with $c_Y(f(x))=c_X(x)$ and $|f(x)|\le C|x|+D$ for
constants $C,D$. Corollary~\ref{cor:comp} shows that complementation is a
parsimonious self-reduction of $\#\mathrm{Jigsaw}$ with $C=1$, $D=0$. It is
computable in a single linear pass.

\begin{theorem}[Freeness]\label{thm:free}
$\comp P=P$ if and only if every clause piece of $P$ is empty.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If all clause pieces are empty there is nothing to flip. Conversely, $\comp P$
has the same shape as $P$. If some clause piece has an input $(i,p)$, the
corresponding position of $\comp P$ holds $(i,p+1)\neq(i,p)$.
\end{proof}

Thus complementation acts freely on the non-degenerate puzzles. That part of the
instance space is partitioned into pairs $\{P,\comp P\}$ of distinct instances
with equal counts.

\section{Mask symmetries and \texorpdfstring{$2$}{2}-adic certificates}

\begin{definition}[Mask-symmetry group]
For a puzzle $P$ let $H_P=\{\mu\in Q_n:\A(P)+\mu=\A(P)\}$, the stabiliser of the
assembly space under translations. It is an $\F$-linear subspace of $Q_n$. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:bij}, every mask $\mu$ with $(\mathrm{id},\mu)\cdot P=P$ lies in
$H_P$, so the results below apply to those masks as well.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[$2$-adic certificate]\label{thm:2adic}
For every puzzle $P$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $|H_P|=2^k$ with $k=\dim H_P$, and $\#P=2^k\cdot|\A(P)/H_P|$; in
  particular $2^k\mid\#P$;
\item $|H_{g\cdot P}|=|H_P|$ for every signed permutation $g$;
\item if $\#P$ is odd then $H_P=\{0\}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(1) $H_P$ acts freely on $\A(P)$ by translation, because $a+\mu=a$ forces
$\mu=0$. All orbits therefore have size $|H_P|$. (2) For $g=(\sigma,\mu_g)$ one
computes $g\cdot(a+\nu)=g\cdot a+\nu\circ\sigma^{-1}$. Together with
$\A(g\cdot P)=g\cdot\A(P)$ this gives
$H_{g\cdot P}=\{\nu\circ\sigma^{-1}:\nu\in H_P\}$. (3) If $2^k$ divides an odd
number then $k=0$.
\end{proof}

Let $v_2$ denote the $2$-adic valuation. The certificate is often sharp: on
random puzzles with $n\le4$, $v_2(\#P)=k$ held in $242$ of $243$ solvable samples.
By (1), the gap $v_2(\#P)-k$ equals $v_2$ of the number of $H_P$-orbits on
$\A(P)$.

\section{The parity of the count}

\begin{theorem}[Mod-$2$ count by signless inclusion--exclusion]\label{thm:ie}
For a set $S$ of clause pieces let $F_S$ be the set of fillings at which every
$c\in S$ fails. Then $\#P\equiv\sum_{S\subseteq P}|F_S|\pmod 2$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Inclusion--exclusion gives $\#P=\sum_S(-1)^{|S|}|F_S|$, and $-1\equiv1\pmod2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Affine-subcube criterion]\label{prop:affine}
Each $F_S$ is empty or an affine subcube. Call $S$ \emph{consistent} if no socket
is forced to both values, and \emph{fully pinning} if every socket occurs in an
input of some clause of $S$. Then
\[
\#P\equiv\big|\{S\subseteq P: S\text{ consistent and fully pinning}\}\big|\pmod2 .
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A clause piece $c$ fails at $a$ exactly when $a_i=p+1$ for every
$(i,p)\in c$. So $F_S$ is cut out by pinning constraints. It is empty on
conflict, and otherwise has $2^{\,n-|V(S)|}$ elements, where $V(S)$ is the set of
pinned sockets. That number is odd exactly when $V(S)=[n]$. Apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:ie}.
\end{proof}

In Example~\ref{ex:main}, $|F_\varnothing|=8$, $|F_{\{c_1\}}|=|F_{\{c_2\}}|=2$
and $|F_{\{c_1,c_2\}}|=0$. No subset is fully pinning, and indeed
$\#P=8-2-2+0=4$ is even.

\section{Encodings: where parsimony breaks}

\subsection{SAT and jigsaw reduce to each other parsimoniously}
A DIMACS CNF on variables $1,\dots,n$ translates to a puzzle by
$+v\mapsto(v,1)$ and $-v\mapsto(v,0)$, preserving shape.

\begin{theorem}[Two-way parsimony]\label{thm:sat}
The translations $\mathrm{CNF}\to\mathrm{Puzzle}$ and
$\mathrm{Puzzle}\to\mathrm{CNF}$ are mutually inverse, size-preserving and
parsimonious.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Hardness transfer]
If a counting problem reduces parsimoniously to $\#$SAT, then it reduces
parsimoniously to $\#$Jigsaw, and hence, for every $k$, to computing
$\#P\bmod k$. Since $\#$SAT is $\#$P-complete under parsimonious reductions,
exact jigsaw assembly counting is $\#$P-complete, and computing $\#P\bmod k$ is
$\mathrm{Mod}_k\mathrm{P}$-hard.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Parsimonious maps with linear size bounds compose to such maps.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Labelled physical assemblies}
To build a physical jigsaw, a framed puzzle with $m$ clause pieces on $n$
sockets is encoded as a pile of labelled pieces. Some of those pieces are
physically interchangeable; the multiplicity factor below records the
relabellings of interchangeable pieces (one family of size $m+2$ and two families
of size $n$).

\begin{theorem}[The encoding breaks parsimony]\label{thm:enc}
The number of labelled physical assemblies is
$\#_{\mathrm{lab}}(P)=\#P\cdot(m+2)!\cdot n!\cdot n!$. Consequently
$\#_{\mathrm{lab}}(P)$ is always even, $\#_{\mathrm{lab}}(P)=0\iff\#P=0$, and if
$\#P>0$ then $\#_{\mathrm{lab}}(P)\neq\#P$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Each mathematical assembly lifts to exactly $(m+2)!(n!)^2$ labelled ones. Since
$(m+2)!\ge2$, the product is even and strictly exceeds $\#P$ when $\#P\ge1$.
\end{proof}

The symmetry $P\mapsto\comp P$ preserves all counting information. The physical
encoding keeps only the zero/nonzero distinction. Indeed, the factor
$(m+2)!(n!)^2$ is divisible by every prime $q\le m+2$, so the encoding erases
every $\mathrm{Mod}_q$ count for such $q$. Piece multiplicities carry counting
information.

\section{Algorithms and experiments}

\textbf{Brute-force count:} enumerate $Q_n$, cost $O(2^n|P|)$.
\textbf{Witness transport:} $a\mapsto g\cdot a$ in $O(n)$ time, landing in
$\A(g\cdot P)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:bij}.
\textbf{Parity by pinning:} for each $S\subseteq P$ propagate forced values,
abort on conflict, count fully pinning subsets; cost $O(2^m|P|)$, preferable when
$m<n$.
\textbf{Mask-symmetry group:} test $\A(P)+\mu=\A(P)$ for each $\mu$; cost
$O(2^n\#P)$.

We tested the results above on enumerated and random instances.
Theorem~\ref{thm:bij} was checked on $1440$ random (puzzle, signed permutation)
pairs, and Theorem~\ref{thm:action} on $300$ random triples.

Theorem~\ref{thm:sat} on $200$ random CNFs. For Example~\ref{ex:main},

Complementation was conjectured to be a parsimonious self-reduction, making the
mod-$2$ count a complementation invariant while the exact count stays

instances and witnesses. The symmetry gives no shortcut to the count. It does

symmetry breaking, and $2$-adic arithmetic information through stabilisers.

types;

a list of literal inputs (i, p) with i a socket in {0,...,n-1} and p a polarity in
{0,1} (0 = blank, 1 = tab).  A choice a in {0,1}^n of variable pieces *assembles*
the puzzle when every clause piece has an input (i, p) with a[i] == p.

  1. Signed-permutation (hyperoctahedral) invariance of the assembly count, via an
     explicit witness bijection.
  2. Compatibility of the action with the group law of signed permutations.
  3. Global complementation is a parsimonious, involutive, size-preserving
     self-reduction; every modular count is a complementation invariant.
  4. Complementation is free away from puzzles whose clause pieces are all empty.
  5. 2-adic divisibility: the polarity-mask symmetry group has order 2^k dividing
     the count; odd counts force a trivial symmetry group; the order is a
     hyperoctahedral invariant.
  6. The mod-2 count via signless inclusion-exclusion, and the affine-subcube
     criterion (only consistent, fully pinning clause subsets contribute).
  7. The labelled physical count count * (m+2)! * n! * n! is always even and is
     never equal to the count of a solvable puzzle.
  8. #SAT <-> #Jigsaw parsimonious translation on DIMACS-style CNFs.

Only the Python standard library is used.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
import random
from typing import Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Lit = Tuple[int, int]
Clause = List[Lit]
Puzzle = List[Clause]
Cube = Tuple[int, ...]
SignedPerm = Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], Tuple[int, ...]]  # (perm, mask)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def fits(a: Cube, lit: Lit) -> bool:
    """A literal input mates with the variable piece at its socket."""
    return a[lit[0]] == lit[1]


def assembles(puzzle: Puzzle, a: Cube) -> bool:
    """Every clause piece has a mating input."""
    return all(any(fits(a, l) for l in c) for c in puzzle)


def cube(n: int) -> Iterable[Cube]:
    return itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=n)


def assemblies(puzzle: Puzzle, n: int) -> List[Cube]:
    return [a for a in cube(n) if assembles(puzzle, a)]


def count(puzzle: Puzzle, n: int) -> int:
    return len(assemblies(puzzle, n))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Hyperoctahedral action
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def act_lit(g: SignedPerm, lit: Lit) -> Lit:
    perm, mask = g
    i, p = lit
    return (perm[i], (p + mask[i]) % 2)


def act_puzzle(g: SignedPerm, puzzle: Puzzle) -> Puzzle:
    return [[act_lit(g, l) for l in c] for c in puzzle]


def act_cube(g: SignedPerm, a: Cube) -> Cube:
    perm, mask = g
    n = len(perm)
    inv = [0] * n
    for i, j in enumerate(perm):
        inv[j] = i
    return tuple((a[inv[j]] + mask[inv[j]]) % 2 for j in range(n))


def mul(g: SignedPerm, h: SignedPerm) -> SignedPerm:
    """g * h acts as 'first h, then g'."""
    gp, gm = g
    hp, hm = h
    n = len(gp)
    perm = tuple(gp[hp[i]] for i in range(n))
    mask = tuple((hm[i] + gm[hp[i]]) % 2 for i in range(n))
    return (perm, mask)


def complement(puzzle: Puzzle, n: int) -> Puzzle:
    """Global tab/blank swap: the signed permutation (id, all-ones)."""
    return act_puzzle((tuple(range(n)), (1,) * n), puzzle)


def all_signed_perms(n: int) -> List[SignedPerm]:
    return [(p, m) for p in itertools.permutations(range(n)) for m in cube(n)]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Mask symmetries and 2-adic divisibility
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def mask_symm(puzzle: Puzzle, n: int) -> List[Cube]:
    """Polarity masks mu whose flip maps the assembly space of P onto itself."""
    A = set(assemblies(puzzle, n))
    out = []
    for mu in cube(n):
        if {tuple((x + y) % 2 for x, y in zip(a, mu)) for a in A} == A:
            out.append(mu)
    return out

    if x == 0:
        return 10 ** 9
    k = 0
    while x % 2 == 0:
        x //= 2
        k += 1
    return k


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Mod-2 inclusion-exclusion and the affine-subcube criterion
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def falsifiers(clauses: Sequence[Clause], n: int) -> int:
    """Number of a falsifying every clause in the given subset."""
    return sum(1 for a in cube(n) if all(not any(fits(a, l) for l in c) for c in clauses))


def mod2_by_inclusion_exclusion(puzzle: Puzzle, n: int) -> int:
    total = 0
    for r in range(len(puzzle) + 1):
        for S in itertools.combinations(puzzle, r):
            total += falsifiers(S, n)
    return total % 2


def pins_consistently_everything(clauses: Sequence[Clause], n: int) -> bool:
    """Falsifying all of S forces a[i] = p+1 for each input (i,p); consistent & full?"""
    pinned: dict[int, int] = {}
    for c in clauses:
        for i, p in c:
            v = (p + 1) % 2
            if pinned.get(i, v) != v:
                return False
            pinned[i] = v
    return len(pinned) == n


def mod2_by_affine_criterion(puzzle: Puzzle, n: int) -> int:
    k = 0
    for r in range(len(puzzle) + 1):
        for S in itertools.combinations(puzzle, r):
            k += pins_consistently_everything(S, n)
    return k % 2


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Encoding: labelled physical assemblies
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def labelled_count(puzzle: Puzzle, n: int) -> int:
    m = len(puzzle)
    return count(puzzle, n) * math.factorial(m + 2) * math.factorial(n) ** 2


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# SAT <-> Jigsaw
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def dimacs_to_puzzle(cnf: List[List[int]]) -> Puzzle:
    """DIMACS literal +v / -v (v >= 1) -> input at socket v-1, polarity 1 / 0."""
    return [[(abs(x) - 1, 1 if x > 0 else 0) for x in c] for c in cnf]


def puzzle_to_dimacs(puzzle: Puzzle) -> List[List[int]]:
    return [[(i + 1) if p == 1 else -(i + 1) for i, p in c] for c in puzzle]


def sat_count(cnf: List[List[int]], n: int) -> int:
    return sum(1 for a in cube(n)
               if all(any((a[abs(x) - 1] == 1) == (x > 0) for x in c) for c in cnf))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def random_puzzle(n: int, m: int, width: int, rng: random.Random) -> Puzzle:
    return [[(rng.randrange(n), rng.randrange(2)) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, width))]
            for _ in range(m)]


def main() -> None:
    rng = random.Random(2026)

    print("=" * 72)
    print("1. A worked example")
    n = 3
    P: Puzzle = [[(0, 1), (1, 1)], [(1, 0), (2, 1)]]
    Pc = complement(P, n)
    print("  P        =", P)
    print("  comp(P)  =", Pc)
    print("  assemblies(P)       =", assemblies(P, n))
    print("  assemblies(comp(P)) =", assemblies(Pc, n))
    print("  counts:", count(P, n), count(Pc, n))

    print("=" * 72)
    print("2. Hyperoctahedral invariance with explicit witness bijection")
    checked = 0
    for _ in range(300):
        n = rng.randint(1, 4)
        Q = random_puzzle(n, rng.randint(0, 5), 3, rng)
        for g in rng.sample(all_signed_perms(n), min(6, 2 ** n * math.factorial(n))):
            A = assemblies(Q, n)
            B = set(assemblies(act_puzzle(g, Q), n))
            image = {act_cube(g, a) for a in A}
            assert image == B and len(image) == len(A)
            checked += 1
    print(f"  {checked} (puzzle, signed permutation) pairs: g maps assemblies(P) onto assemblies(gP)")

    print("=" * 72)
    print("3. Group law: (g*h).P == g.(h.P)")
    for _ in range(300):
        n = rng.randint(1, 4)
        Q = random_puzzle(n, 4, 3, rng)
        G = all_signed_perms(n)
        g, h = rng.choice(G), rng.choice(G)
        assert act_puzzle(mul(g, h), Q) == act_puzzle(g, act_puzzle(h, Q))
    print("  verified on 300 random triples")

    print("=" * 72)
    print("4. Complementation: parsimonious, involutive, size preserving, free")
    for n in range(1, 4):
        lits = [(i, p) for i in range(n) for p in (0, 1)]
        clauses = [list(c) for r in range(0, 3) for c in itertools.combinations(lits, r)]
        tot = 0
        for Q in itertools.product(clauses, repeat=2):
            Q = list(map(list, Q))
            Qc = complement(Q, n)
            assert count(Q, n) == count(Qc, n)
            for k in (2, 3, 5):
                assert count(Q, n) % k == count(Qc, n) % k
            assert complement(Qc, n) == Q
            assert sum(map(len, Q)) == sum(map(len, Qc))
            assert (Qc == Q) == all(len(c) == 0 for c in Q)
            tot += 1
        print(f"  n={n}: all {tot} two-clause puzzles (clause width <= 2) pass")

    print("=" * 72)
    print("5. 2-adic certificates from polarity-mask symmetries")
    stats = {"equal": 0, "gap": 0}
    for _ in range(400):
        n = rng.randint(1, 4)
        Q = random_puzzle(n, rng.randint(0, 4), 3, rng)
        c = count(Q, n)
        H = mask_symm(Q, n)
        k = int(math.log2(len(H)))
        assert 2 ** k == len(H) and c % len(H) == 0
        if c % 2 == 1:
            assert len(H) == 1
        g = rng.choice(all_signed_perms(n))
        assert len(mask_symm(act_puzzle(g, Q), n)) == len(H)
        if c > 0:
            stats["equal" if v2(c) == k else "gap"] += 1
    print("  |H| = 2^k divides count, odd count => H trivial, |H| invariant: OK")
    print(f"  among solvable samples: v2(count) = k in {stats['equal']}, strict gap in {stats['gap']}")

    print("=" * 72)
    print("6. Mod-2 count: signless inclusion-exclusion and affine-subcube criterion")
    for _ in range(300):
        n = rng.randint(1, 4)
        Q = random_puzzle(n, rng.randint(0, 5), 3, rng)
        c2 = count(Q, n) % 2
        assert c2 == mod2_by_inclusion_exclusion(Q, n) == mod2_by_affine_criterion(Q, n)
    print("  three ways of computing count mod 2 agree on 300 random puzzles")

    print("=" * 72)
    print("7. The encoding breaks parsimony")
    for n, Q in [(3, P), (2, [[(0, 1)], [(1, 0)]]), (2, [[(0, 1)], [(0, 0)]])]:
        c, L = count(Q, n), labelled_count(Q, n)
        print(f"  n={n}, m={len(Q)}: count={c:3d}  labelled={L:8d}  even={L % 2 == 0}"
              f"  parsimonious={L == c}")

    print("=" * 72)
    print("8. #SAT <-> #Jigsaw")
    for _ in range(200):
        n = rng.randint(1, 5)
        cnf = [[rng.choice([1, -1]) * rng.randint(1, n) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 3))]
               for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 6))]
        Q = dimacs_to_puzzle(cnf)
        assert count(Q, n) == sat_count(cnf, n)
        assert puzzle_to_dimacs(Q) == cnf
    print("  translations are mutually inverse and count-preserving on 200 random CNFs")
    print("=" * 72)
    print("All checks passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

        clauses = [list(c) for r in range(0, 3) for c in itertools.combinations(lits, r)]
        tot = 0
        for Q in itertools.product(clauses, repeat=2):
            Q = list(map(list, Q))
            Qc = complement(Q, n)
            assert count(Q, n) == count(Qc, n)
            for k in (2, 3, 5):
                assert count(Q, n) % k == count(Qc, n) % k
            assert complement(Qc, n) == Q
            assert sum(map(len, Q)) == sum(map(len, Qc))
            assert (Qc == Q) == all(len(c) == 0 for c in Q)
            tot += 1
        print(f"  n={n}: all {tot} two-clause puzzles (clause width <= 2) pass")

    print("=" * 72)
    print("5. 2-adic certificates from polarity-mask symmetries")
    stats = {"equal": 0, "gap": 0}
    for _ in range(400):
        n = rng.randint(1, 4)
        Q = random_puzzle(n, rng.randint(0, 4), 3, rng)
        c = count(Q, n)
        H = mask_symm(Q, n)
        k = int(math.log2(len(H)))
        assert 2 ** k == len(H) and c % len(H) == 0
        if c % 2 == 1:
            assert len(H) == 1
        g = rng.choice(all_signed_perms(n))
        assert len(mask_symm(act_puzzle(g, Q), n)) == len(H)
        if c > 0:
            stats["equal" if v2(c) == k else "gap"] += 1
    print("  |H| = 2^k divides count, odd count => H trivial, |H| invariant: OK")
    print(f"  among solvable samples: v2(count) = k in {stats['equal']}, strict gap in {stats['gap']}")

    print("=" * 72)
    print("6. Mod-2 count: signless inclusion-exclusion and affine-subcube criterion")
    for _ in range(300):
        n = rng.randint(1, 4)
        Q = random_puzzle(n, rng.randint(0, 5), 3, rng)
        c2 = count(Q, n) % 2
        assert c2 == mod2_by_inclusion_exclusion(Q, n) == mod2_by_affine_criterion(Q, n)
    print("  three ways of computing count mod 2 agree on 300 random puzzles")

    print("=" * 72)
    print("7. The encoding breaks parsimony")
    for n, Q in [(3, P), (2, [[(0, 1)], [(1, 0)]]), (2, [[(0, 1)], [(0, 0)]])]:
        c, L = count(Q, n), labelled_count(Q, n)
        print(f"  n={n}, m={len(Q)}: count={c:3d}  labelled={L:8d}  even={L % 2 == 0}"
              f"  parsimonious={L == c}")

    print("=" * 72)
    print("8. #SAT <-> #Jigsaw")
    for _ in range(200):
        n = rng.randint(1, 5)
        cnf = [[rng.choice([1, -1]) * rng.randint(1, n) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 3))]
               for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 6))]
        Q = dimacs_to_puzzle(cnf)
        assert count(Q, n) == sat_count(cnf, n)
        assert puzzle_to_dimacs(Q) == cnf
    print("  translations are mutually inverse and count-preserving on 200 random CNFs")
    print("=" * 72)
    print("All checks passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Witness Transport under a Signed Permutation
algorithms.description: Given a signed permutation g = (sigma, mu), a puzzle P and an assembly a of P, compute the assembly g.a of g.P via (g.a)_{sigma(i)} = a_i + mu_i. Correctness is the literal-level transport identity: g.(i,p) fits g.a iff (i,p) fits a, by cancellation in Z/2. The inverse map b -> (b_{sigma(i)} - mu_i)_i recovers a, so this is a bijection of assembly spaces. Transforming the puzzle costs O(|P|) and transporting one witness costs O(n). Global complementation is the case sigma = id, mu = all-ones.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: sigma in S_n, mu in {0,1}^n, puzzle P, assembly a
1. for each clause c in P, for each connector (i,p) in c: replace by (sigma(i), p XOR mu_i)   // g.P
2. for i = 1..n: b[sigma(i)] <- a_i XOR mu_i                                    // g.a
3. (check) b assembles g.P and inverse(b) = a, where inverse(b)_i = b[sigma(i)] XOR mu_i
OUTPUT: g.P, b
algorithms.code:
from typing import List, Tuple
Lit = Tuple[int, int]
Puzzle = List[List[Lit]]
SignedPerm = Tuple[List[int], List[int]]   # (sigma, mu), 0-indexed sockets

def act_puzzle(g: SignedPerm, P: Puzzle) -> Puzzle:
    sigma, mu = g
    return [[(sigma[i], (p + mu[i]) % 2) for (i, p) in c] for c in P]

def act_cube(g: SignedPerm, a: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    sigma, mu = g
    b = [0] * len(a)
    for i, ai in enumerate(a):
        b[sigma[i]] = (ai + mu[i]) % 2
    return b

def inv_cube(g: SignedPerm, b: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    sigma, mu = g
    return [(b[sigma[i]] - mu[i]) % 2 for i in range(len(b))]

def assembles(P: Puzzle, a: List[int]) -> bool:
    return all(any(a[i] == p for i, p in c) for c in P)

def transport(g: SignedPerm, P: Puzzle, a: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """Map an assembly of P to an assembly of g.P (the witness bijection)."""
    assert assembles(P, a)
    b = act_cube(g, a)
    assert assembles(act_puzzle(g, P), b) and inv_cube(g, b) == a
    return b

if __name__ == "__main__":
    P = [[(0, 1), (1, 1)], [(1, 0), (2, 1)]]
    comp = ([0, 1, 2], [1, 1, 1])
    print(transport(comp, P, [0, 1, 1]))   # -> [1, 0, 0]

algorithms.name: Parity of the Assembly Count by Consistent Full Pinning
algorithms.description: Signless inclusion-exclusion gives #P = sum over clause subsets S of |F_S| (mod 2), where F_S is the set of fillings falsifying every clause of S. Falsifying a connector (i,p) pins socket i to 1-p, so F_S is empty on a conflict and otherwise a subcube of size 2^(n - #pinned). That size is odd exactly when all n sockets are pinned. The algorithm counts consistent, fully pinning subsets modulo 2. It runs in O(2^m |P|) time for m clause pieces, which beats the O(2^n |P|) brute force when m < n.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: puzzle P with clauses c_1..c_m on n sockets
parity <- 0
for each subset S of {c_1..c_m}:
    forced <- empty map; ok <- true
    for each (i,p) in clauses of S:
        v <- 1 - p
        if forced[i] defined and forced[i] != v: ok <- false
        forced[i] <- v
    if ok and |forced| = n: parity <- parity XOR 1
OUTPUT: parity  (= #P mod 2)

algorithms.name: Mask-Symmetry Group and 2-adic Certificate
algorithms.description: Computes H_P = {mu : A(P) + mu = A(P)}, the stabiliser of the assembly space under cube translations. H_P is an F_2-subspace, so |H_P| = 2^k, and it acts freely on A(P). Hence #P = 2^k times the number of orbits, and 2^k divides #P. The order is invariant under signed permutations because g conjugates translation by nu into translation by nu composed with sigma^{-1}. Cost O(2^n #P n) after enumerating A(P).

"""Side-by-side drawing of the 3-cube: assemblies of a puzzle and of its complement."""
from __future__ import annotations
import itertools
from typing import List, Tuple
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Lit = Tuple[int, int]
Puzzle = List[List[Lit]]

def assembles(P: Puzzle, a: Tuple[int, ...]) -> bool:
    return all(any(a[i] == p for i, p in c) for c in P)

def complement(P: Puzzle) -> Puzzle:
    return [[(i, 1 - p) for i, p in c] for c in P]

def project(a: Tuple[int, ...]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    x, y, z = a
    return x + 0.45 * z, y + 0.35 * z

def draw(ax, P: Puzzle, title: str) -> None:
    corners = list(itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=3))
    for a in corners:
        for i in range(3):
            if a[i] == 0:
                b = list(a); b[i] = 1; b = tuple(b)
                (x1, y1), (x2, y2) = project(a), project(b)
                ax.plot([x1, x2], [y1, y2], color="#888", lw=1)
    for a in corners:
        x, y = project(a)
        ok = assembles(P, a)
        ax.scatter([x], [y], s=520, color="#2ecc71" if ok else "#dfe6e9", edgecolor="k", zorder=3)
        ax.text(x, y, "".join(map(str, a)), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, zorder=4)
    n_sol = sum(assembles(P, a) for a in corners)
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\nassembly count = {n_sol}")
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    P: Puzzle = [[(0, 1), (1, 1)], [(1, 0), (2, 1)]]   # (x1 or x2) and (not x2 or x3)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5))
    draw(axes[0], P, "P = (x1 ∨ x2) ∧ (¬x2 ∨ x3)")
    draw(axes[1], complement(P), "complement: (¬x1 ∨ ¬x2) ∧ (x2 ∨ ¬x3)")
    fig.suptitle("Complementation moves the solution set by the antipodal map of the cube")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

"""Histogram of the 2-adic gap v2(#P) - log2|H_P| over random small puzzles."""
from __future__ import annotations
import itertools, math, random
from collections import Counter
from typing import List, Tuple
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Puzzle = List[List[Tuple[int, int]]]

def sols(P: Puzzle, n: int) -> List[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    return [a for a in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=n)
            if all(any(a[i] == p for i, p in c) for c in P)]

def mask_symm_order(S: List[Tuple[int, ...]], n: int) -> int:
    A = set(S)
    return sum(1 for mu in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=n)
               if {tuple((x + y) % 2 for x, y in zip(a, mu)) for a in A} == A)

def v2(x: int) -> int:
    k = 0
    while x % 2 == 0:
        x //= 2; k += 1
    return k

if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = random.Random(1)
    gaps: Counter = Counter(); ks: Counter = Counter()
    for _ in range(3000):
        n = rng.randint(1, 4)
        P = [[(rng.randrange(n), rng.randrange(2)) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 3))]
             for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 4))]
        S = sols(P, n)
        if not S:
            continue
        k = int(math.log2(mask_symm_order(S, n)))
        gaps[v2(len(S)) - k] += 1; ks[k] += 1
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
    ax[0].bar(list(gaps.keys()), list(gaps.values()), color="#6c5ce7")
    ax[0].set_xlabel("gap  v2(#P) − log2|H_P|"); ax[0].set_ylabel("puzzles")
    ax[0].set_title("The 2-adic certificate is almost always sharp")
    ax[1].bar(list(ks.keys()), list(ks.values()), color="#00b894")
    ax[1].set_xlabel("k = log2 |H_P|"); ax[1].set_title("Order of the mask-symmetry group")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# Turning a Puzzle Inside Out

*A guided tour of why swapping every tab for a blank never changes how many ways a jigsaw can be finished, and of where counting information really gets lost.*

## 1. A jigsaw that is secretly a logic formula

A **framed puzzle** has $n$ sockets. Each socket receives either a tab ($1$) or a blank ($0$), so a filling is a point $a\in\{0,1\}^n$, a corner of the $n$-dimensional cube. A **clause piece** carries connectors $(i,p)$: socket $i$, polarity $p$. It snaps in when at least one connector mates, i.e. $a_i = p$. The puzzle is **assembled** when every clause piece snaps in.

So a puzzle *is* a CNF formula, and assemblies are satisfying assignments. The **assembly count** $\#P$ is exactly the quantity computed by [#SAT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharp-SAT).

<details><summary>Background: decision, counting and parity classes</summary>

Deciding whether $\#P>0$ is SAT, which is [NP-complete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook%E2%80%93Levin_theorem). Computing $\#P$ exactly is [#P-complete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E2%99%AFP-complete) (Valiant, 1979). Computing $\#P \bmod 2$ is complete for [⊕P](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_P). By [Toda's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toda%27s_theorem) the whole polynomial hierarchy lies in $\mathrm{P}^{\#\mathrm{P}}$, and the proof runs through parity counting. A **parsimonious** reduction preserves the exact number of witnesses, and hence every modular count.
</details>

Try it yourself: the laboratory below starts with $(x_1\lor x_2)\land(\lnot x_2\lor x_3)$, which has four assemblies.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

## 2. The flip

Press **Complement**. Every connector $(i,p)$ becomes $(i,1-p)$. The green corners move, but their number stays the same: each new assembly is the bitwise negation of an old one.

{{visualization:0}}

> **Complementation Theorem.** $a \models P \iff a+\mathbf 1 \models \overline P$. Hence $\#\overline P = \#P$, and $\#\overline P\equiv \#P \pmod k$ for every $k$. The map is linear-time, size-preserving and involutive: a **parsimonious self-reduction**.

## 3. A whole group of flips

The flip is one element of the **hyperoctahedral group** $B_n=(\mathbb Z/2)^n\rtimes S_n$ of signed permutations $g=(\sigma,\mu)$. Each one relabels socket $i$ as $\sigma(i)$ and flips the polarity where $\mu_i=1$. Use *Random signed permutation* in the laboratory and watch the "history of counts" row: it never changes.

<details><summary>Click to reveal the proof of hyperoctahedral invariance</summary>

Define $g\cdot(i,p) = (\sigma(i), p+\mu_i)$ and $(g\cdot a)_{\sigma(i)} = a_i+\mu_i$. Then $g\cdot(i,p)$ fits $g\cdot a$ iff $a_i+\mu_i = p+\mu_i$ iff $a_i=p$. Applying this connector by connector and clause by clause gives $g\cdot a\models g\cdot P \iff a\models P$. The map $a\mapsto g\cdot a$ is a bijection of the cube with inverse $(g^{-1}b)_i = b_{\sigma(i)}-\mu_i$, so it restricts to a bijection of assembly spaces. Compatibility with the group law, $(gh)\cdot P = g\cdot(h\cdot P)$, holds connector by connector because $\mu_{h,i}+\mu_{g,\sigma_h(i)}$ is the mask of $gh$.
</details>

The witness bijection is completely explicit:

{{algorithm:0}}

**Freeness.** $\overline P = P$ happens only when every clause piece is empty, because a single connector $(i,p)$ becomes $(i,1-p)$. Away from these degenerate puzzles, instances come in distinct pairs $\{P,\overline P\}$ with equal counts.

## 4. Symmetry forces powers of two

Let $H_P$ be the set of masks $\mu$ with $\mathcal A(P)+\mu = \mathcal A(P)$. It is a subgroup of $(\mathbb Z/2)^n$, so $|H_P| = 2^k$. It acts **freely** on the assemblies.

> **2-adic Certificate Theorem.** $2^k$ divides $\#P$; $|H_{g\cdot P}| = |H_P|$ for every signed permutation; an odd count forces $H_P$ to be trivial.

In the laboratory, try the puzzle `1 -1 | 2` with $n=3$. Socket 3 never matters, and neither does socket 1, so $H_P$ has order $4$ and $\#P=4$.

{{algorithm:2}}

How sharp is the certificate? Almost always exactly sharp:

{{visualization:1}}

<details><summary>Why the gap is the parity of the number of orbits</summary>
Since every $H_P$-orbit has exactly $2^k$ elements, $\#P = 2^k\cdot|\mathcal A(P)/H_P|$. Thus $v_2(\#P) - k = v_2(\#\text{orbits})$, and the certificate is sharp exactly when the number of orbits is odd.
</details>

## 5. Parity without counting

Inclusion–exclusion gives $\#P = \sum_S (-1)^{|S|}|F_S|$, where $F_S$ is the set of fillings at which every clause in $S$ fails. Modulo 2 the signs vanish. Each $F_S$ is empty or a subcube of size $2^{\,n-\#\text{pinned sockets}}$, which is odd only when every socket is pinned. Panel 5 of the laboratory lists every subset.

> **Affine-subcube criterion.** $\#P \equiv \#\{S : S \text{ consistent and pins all } n \text{ sockets}\} \pmod 2$.

{{algorithm:1}}

## 6. Where parsimony actually breaks

DIMACS formulas and puzzles translate into each other **parsimoniously**, so every hardness result for counting SAT solutions, exact or modular, transfers to jigsaws. The *physical* encoding behaves differently. Labelled pieces turn each assembly into $(m+2)!\,n!\,n!$ labelled assemblies:

$$\#_{\text{lab}}(P) = \#P\cdot(m+2)!\cdot n!\cdot n!.$$

This number is always even, and it differs from $\#P$ on every solvable puzzle. The encoding keeps solvability and erases the parity (watch the "labelled physical count" row in the laboratory). **Piece multiplicities carry counting information.** The mathematics preserves it and the packaging destroys it.

## 7. Run every check yourself

The script below exhaustively or randomly tests each of the statements above on small instances: invariance, the group law, freeness, the 2-adic certificate, the three parity computations, the encoding formula and SAT ↔ jigsaw parsimony.

{{demo:0}}

<details><summary>Open questions</summary>

* A Burnside census of hyperoctahedral orbits of two-clause puzzles over signed cycle types.
* When exactly is $v_2(\#P) = \log_2|H_P|$?
* Which structured puzzle families have polynomial-time parity through the pinning criterion?
* Physical encodings with odd multiplicity factor, which would keep modular counts intact.
</details>
